package.name: Algorithms
package.description: Generic algorithms over slices and mutable slices

modules.name: Find
modules.header:
Linear queries over a sequence that is in no particular order.
Everything here reads a `T[..]` and returns an answer about it. A search that found something answers with the
index it found, as an optional `uint?`, because "not found" is an ordinary outcome and a sentinel index is a bug
waiting for the one sequence long enough to reach it. An empty slice is not a special case anywhere: it contains
nothing, satisfies every universal claim, and matches no search.
The value-based queries need `==` on the element type and nothing more, so a type with equality but no ordering
can use them. The predicate-based ones need nothing at all — the caller's function supplies the test — and the
ordered searches live in `Search`, which needs `<`.
A predicate is an ordinary function value. Rux has no closures, so it carries no captured state: anything it needs
beyond the element has to be reachable from the function itself.
Nothing here allocates, and nothing here writes. Every one of these is a single pass unless it says otherwise.

modules.name: Fold
modules.header:
Reducing a sequence to one value, and mapping one sequence onto another.
A fold is the general form: an accumulator, a starting value, and a function that folds each element into it. The
accumulator's type is independent of the element's, so the same operation both sums a sequence of numbers and
builds something else entirely out of one.
The numeric forms are folds with the function already chosen. They take the starting value rather than assuming
one, because a generic `T` has no zero this package could name: nothing here requires a type to say what its
additive identity is, and inventing one would be wrong for every type that has no such thing. Passing `0` costs a
caller nothing and keeps the operation honest about what it does.
Overflow is the element type's business. `Sum` adds with `+`, so a sum that does not fit behaves exactly as `+`
behaves on that type — these do not check, and a caller who needs checking folds `AddChecked` instead. That is
the fold's whole reason for being general.
Nothing here allocates.

modules.name: Heap
modules.header:
A binary max-heap laid out in the sequence itself, with no node structure and no allocation.
The heap property is an arrangement rather than a type: element `i` is at least as large as elements `2i+1` and
`2i+2`, which puts the largest element at the front and lets the largest be removed, or a new element added, in
time proportional to the logarithm of the length. That is what a priority queue is, and it is why these operations
are here rather than in a container — any sequence a caller already has can be one.
The arrangement is not an order. A heap is not sorted, and only its first element is where a sorted sequence would
put it. `SortHeap` turns one into the other, which is what heapsort is.
Every operation here takes the whole heap as a view and works within it. Growing and shrinking are the caller's:
`PushHeap` is told about an element already appended, and `PopHeap` leaves the removed element at the end for the
caller to drop. That keeps this package out of the business of owning storage, which it is not in anywhere.
Requires `<` on the element type, or a three-way comparison for the `By` forms. Nothing here allocates.

modules.name: MinMax
modules.header:
The smallest and largest elements of a sequence, and clamping a value into a range.
Every search here answers with an index rather than a value, because the index is the more useful answer and the
value is one dereference away. An empty slice has no smallest element, so the answer is `none` rather than a
sentinel index or a default-constructed value that was never in the sequence.
Ties go to the first: `MinIndex` reports the earliest of several equal smallest elements, and `MaxIndex` the
earliest of several equal largest ones. That is a promise rather than an accident, and it is what makes a sort
built on these predictable.
The plain forms need `<` on the element type. The `By` forms take a three-way comparison instead, which is what to
use when the element has no ordering of its own, or when the wanted order is not its own.

modules.name: Modify
modules.header:
Rearranging a sequence in place, and moving elements between sequences.
Everything that writes takes a `var T[..]`; everything that only reads takes a `T[..]`. Nothing here
resizes anything, because none of these own the storage they work on. The removals compact survivors toward the
front and report how many are left, and it is the caller — who does own the storage — that shortens it.
What is left past the reported length after a removal is unspecified. It is neither cleared nor preserved: the
elements there were moved from, and reading them back is reading whatever the compaction happened to leave. For a
`Copy` element that is a stale duplicate; for anything else it is a value with no owner.
A rotation and a reversal need no scratch storage at all, which is why they are here rather than in an allocating
layer: a rotation is three reversals, and that is the whole of it.

modules.name: Search
modules.header:
Searching a sequence that is already in order, and asking whether it is.
Everything here assumes the slice is sorted by the same order the search uses. That is the caller's promise, and
nothing checks it on the way in: checking would cost the linear scan the binary search exists to avoid. A search
over an unsorted slice does not fail — it answers, and the answer is meaningless. `IsSorted` is there for a
caller who wants to check, once, where checking is worth it.
A bound is a position rather than an element: `LowerBound` is the first position where the value could be inserted
without breaking the order, and `UpperBound` is the last. Between them lie exactly the elements equal to it, which
is what `EqualRange` returns in one pass. All three answer for a value that is not present at all — the answer is
an empty range at the position it would go.
The plain forms need `<` on the element type. The `By` forms take a three-way comparison, which is what to use for
a type with no ordering of its own or an order that is not its own. Every `By` form must be given the same order
the slice was sorted by; a different one gives a meaningless answer just as an unsorted slice does.
Nothing here allocates or writes.

modules.name: Sort
modules.header:
Sorting: putting a sequence in order, in place, with no storage but its own.
`Sort` is an introsort — quicksort with a three-way partition, falling back to heapsort once the recursion budget
is spent and to insertion sort on small partitions. Each part covers the others' weakness. Quicksort is the
fastest of the three on ordinary input and the only one that degrades to quadratic on input chosen to defeat its
pivot rule; heapsort never degrades and is slower on everything; insertion sort beats both below about sixteen
elements, where choosing a pivot costs more than the sorting does. The result has a genuine O(n log n) worst case
with no auxiliary storage, which no one of the three has alone.
**The worst case, precisely.** Comparisons are O(n log n) for every input, with no exceptions and nothing
probabilistic about it: the depth budget is `2 * floor(log2 n)`, and a range still unsorted when it runs out is
handed to heapsort, which is O(n log n) unconditionally. Auxiliary storage is O(1) — one pivot and a few indices.
Stack depth is O(log n) frames, about sixty-four for any addressable length, because the recursive call always
takes the smaller side of a partition while the larger is handled by the loop. None of that depends on the input
being random, and there are no randomized pivots to make it depend on the run.
**Sorting is not stable.** Equivalent elements may come out in a different order than they went in. It is
deterministic — the same input always gives the same output and the same number of comparisons — but a caller
who needs equal elements to keep their original order needs a stable sort, which needs somewhere to put things.
The plain forms require `<` on the element type and nothing else, under the same strict-weak-ordering contract as
`Search`: equivalence is derived as neither element being less than the other, so a type that orders without
defining `==` sorts fine. The `By` forms take a three-way comparison instead, for a sequence ordered by something
other than its element type's own `<`.
The `By` machinery below mirrors the operator-based helpers rather than sharing them. A generic function cannot be
used as a value in Rux, so the operator forms cannot pass `<` as a comparator into one shared implementation, and
threading a runtime flag instead would put a branch in the innermost comparison of every sort — the one place it
would be felt. When generic functions become usable as values, the two sets collapse into one.

modules.name: Stable
modules.header:
Stable sorting: putting a sequence in order while leaving equal elements in the order they arrived.
`Sort` is faster and needs no storage at all, and for most sequences the difference between equal elements is not
observable. It becomes observable the moment a second key is involved: sort a table by one column, then by
another, and only a stable sort leaves the first ordering intact within each group of the second. That is what
this is for, and it is the only reason to pay for it.
The price is storage. A merge cannot be done in place without either quadratic movement or an amount of index
arithmetic that no one should maintain, so this asks the caller for scratch storage as long as the sequence and
merges into it. Asking rather than allocating is deliberate: this package allocates nothing anywhere, which is
what lets it be used where allocation is not available, and a caller who has a buffer already should not have a
second one taken behind their back.
The sort is a bottom-up merge: insertion sort over short runs first, then merges of doubling width, alternating
between the sequence and the scratch so that nothing is copied merely to move it back. An odd number of merge
passes ends with the answer in the scratch, and only then is it copied home.
Comparisons are O(n log n) for every input — there is no bad case here at all, unlike a quicksort — and the
movement is the same. What it costs over `Sort` is the storage and about a constant factor.

items.name: Contains
items.signature: pub func Contains<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether any element of `items` equals `value`.
doc.markdown:
Whether any element of `items` equals `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. An empty slice contains nothing, so this is false.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first match, and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether any element equals `value`

items.name: Count
items.signature: pub func Count<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint

doc.summary: How many elements of `items` equal `value`.
doc.markdown:
How many elements of `items` equal `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. An empty slice gives zero.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: how many elements equal `value`

items.name: IndexOf
items.signature: pub func IndexOf<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of the first element of `items` equal to `value`.
doc.markdown:
The index of the first element of `items` equal to `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. Reports `none` when no element matches, including for an
empty slice.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first match, and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the first index holding `value`, or `none`

items.name: LastIndexOf
items.signature: pub func LastIndexOf<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of the last element of `items` equal to `value`.
doc.markdown:
The index of the last element of `items` equal to `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. Reports `none` when no element matches.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first match from the end, and allocates
nothing.
doc.returns: the last index holding `value`, or `none`

items.name: IndexWhere
items.signature: pub func IndexWhere<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of the first element of `items` that `predicate` accepts.
doc.markdown:
The index of the first element of `items` that `predicate` accepts.
`items` is borrowed and read; `predicate` is called once per element until it accepts one. Reports `none` when
it accepts none.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: the first index whose element satisfies `predicate`, or `none`

items.name: LastIndexWhere
items.signature: pub func LastIndexWhere<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of the last element of `items` that `predicate` accepts.
doc.markdown:
The index of the last element of `items` that `predicate` accepts.
`items` is borrowed and read; `predicate` is called once per element from the end until it accepts one. Reports
`none` when it accepts none.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: the last index whose element satisfies `predicate`, or `none`

items.name: CountWhere
items.signature: pub func CountWhere<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> uint

doc.summary: How many elements of `items` the predicate accepts.
doc.markdown:
How many elements of `items` the predicate accepts.
`items` is borrowed and read; `predicate` is called once per element. An empty slice gives zero.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: how many elements satisfy `predicate`

items.name: AllOf
items.signature: pub func AllOf<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `predicate` accepts every element of `items`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `predicate` accepts every element of `items`.
`items` is borrowed and read. An empty slice satisfies this, as it satisfies every universal claim: there is no
element that fails.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first rejection, and allocates nothing
beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: whether every element satisfies `predicate`; true for an empty sequence

items.name: AnyOf
items.signature: pub func AnyOf<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `predicate` accepts at least one element of `items`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `predicate` accepts at least one element of `items`.
`items` is borrowed and read. An empty slice does not satisfy this: there is no element that passes.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first acceptance, and allocates nothing
beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: whether any element satisfies `predicate`; false for an empty sequence

items.name: NoneOf
items.signature: pub func NoneOf<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `predicate` accepts no element of `items`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `predicate` accepts no element of `items`.
`items` is borrowed and read. An empty slice satisfies this, for the same reason it satisfies `AllOf`.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first acceptance, and allocates nothing
beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: whether no element satisfies `predicate`; true for an empty sequence

items.name: Mismatch
items.signature: pub func Mismatch<T>(left: T[..], right: T[..]) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of the first position where `left` and `right` differ.
doc.markdown:
The index of the first position where `left` and `right` differ.
Both are borrowed and read. Reports `none` when neither runs out before a difference is found and the two are
equal for their whole common length — so two slices of different lengths that agree on the shorter one report
the shorter length, and two identical slices report `none`.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shorter length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the first index where the two differ, or `none` when neither runs out first

items.name: SequenceEqual
items.signature: pub func SequenceEqual<T>(left: T[..], right: T[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `left` and `right` hold the same elements in the same order.
doc.markdown:
Whether `left` and `right` hold the same elements in the same order.
Both are borrowed and read. Different lengths are never equal, and two empty slices are, whatever their data
pointers hold.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shorter length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether both hold the same elements in the same order

items.name: Compare
items.signature: pub func Compare<T>(left: T[..], right: T[..]) -> Ordering

doc.summary: How `left` orders against `right`, element by element.
doc.markdown:
How `left` orders against `right`, element by element.
Both are borrowed and read. The comparison is lexicographic, which is the order a dictionary uses: the first
position where the two differ decides, and if neither differs before one runs out, the shorter is the smaller.
Two equal-length slices that never differ are `Equal`.
Requires `<` and `==` on the element type. Use `CompareBy` where the element has no ordering of its own or the
wanted order is not its own.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shorter length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: how `left` orders against `right`, comparing element by element then by length

items.name: CompareBy
items.signature: pub func CompareBy<T>(left: T[..], right: T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> Ordering

doc.summary: How `left` orders against `right`, with `compare` deciding each pair.
doc.markdown:
How `left` orders against `right`, with `compare` deciding each pair.
Both slices are borrowed and read; `compare` is called at most once per position of the shorter one. Lexicographic
exactly as `Compare` is, and the way to order a sequence whose elements have no `<` of their own — or to order it
by something other than their own.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the shorter length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `compare` does.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

doc.returns: how `left` orders against `right` under `compare`, then by length

items.name: Fold
items.signature: pub func Fold<T, A>(items: T[..], initial: A, combine: func(A, T) -> A) -> A

doc.summary: Folds every element of `items` into an accumulator, left to right.
doc.markdown:
Folds every element of `items` into an accumulator, left to right.
`items` is borrowed and read; `initial` is read by value and returned when the sequence is empty; `combine` is
called once per element with the accumulator so far and the element. The accumulator's type is independent of the
element's.
Left to right is part of the contract rather than an implementation detail: a `combine` that is not associative
gives a different answer in the other direction, and callers depend on the order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `combine` does.

params.name: combine
params.markdown: how to fold an element into the running value

doc.returns: the value left after folding every element into it

items.name: FoldRight
items.signature: pub func FoldRight<T, A>(items: T[..], initial: A, combine: func(A, T) -> A) -> A

doc.summary: Folds every element of `items` into an accumulator, right to left.
doc.markdown:
Folds every element of `items` into an accumulator, right to left.
`items` is borrowed and read; `initial` is read by value and returned when the sequence is empty; `combine` is
called once per element with the accumulator so far and the element, starting from the last.
The mirror of `Fold`, and a different answer for any `combine` that is not associative.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `combine` does.

params.name: combine
params.markdown: how to fold an element into the running value

doc.returns: the value left after folding every element into it, from the end

items.name: Sum
items.signature: pub func Sum<T>(items: T[..], initial: T) -> T

doc.summary: The sum of `initial` and every element of `items`.
doc.markdown:
The sum of `initial` and every element of `items`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `initial` is read by value and is what an empty sequence gives back. The starting
value is asked for rather than assumed, because a generic element type has no zero this package could name.
Requires `+` on the element type. Overflow behaves exactly as `+` does on that type: this does not check, and a
caller who needs checking folds a checked addition instead.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: `initial` plus every element

items.name: Product
items.signature: pub func Product<T>(items: T[..], initial: T) -> T

doc.summary: The product of `initial` and every element of `items`.
doc.markdown:
The product of `initial` and every element of `items`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `initial` is read by value and is what an empty sequence gives back — which is why
it must be one rather than zero for the answer to mean anything.
Requires `*` on the element type. Overflow behaves exactly as `*` does on that type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: `initial` times every element

items.name: Transform
items.signature: pub func Transform<T, U>(destination: var U[..], source: T[..], transform: func(T) -> U) -> bool

doc.summary: Writes `transform` of each element of `source` into `destination`.
doc.markdown:
Writes `transform` of each element of `source` into `destination`.
`source` is borrowed and read; `destination` is borrowed mutably and written; `transform` is called once per
element. The two sequences may have different element types, and may be the same storage when they do not.
Reports false, having written nothing, when the two lengths differ — for the same reason `CopyTo` does: a
partial result is worse than a refused one when the caller cannot tell how far it got.
Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `transform` does.

params.name: transform
params.markdown: how to turn a source element into a destination one

doc.returns: whether `destination` was long enough to hold every result

items.name: MakeHeap
items.signature: pub func MakeHeap<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Rearranges `items` into a max-heap.
doc.markdown:
Rearranges `items` into a max-heap.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. Fewer than two elements are already a heap. The arrangement is not an
order: only the first element ends up where a sorted sequence would put it.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length — linear, not `n log n`, because sifting from the bottom up
does most of its work on the short subtrees near the leaves. Allocates nothing.

items.name: PushHeap
items.signature: pub func PushHeap<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Restores the heap property after an element has been appended to `items`.
doc.markdown:
Restores the heap property after an element has been appended to `items`.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; it must be the whole heap including the new last element, and
everything before that element must already be a heap. An empty view does nothing.
The caller appends and this repairs, because appending is the storage owner's business.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing.

items.name: PopHeap
items.signature: pub func PopHeap<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Moves the largest element of `items` to its end and restores the heap property over the rest.
doc.markdown:
Moves the largest element of `items` to its end and restores the heap property over the rest.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. Afterwards the largest element sits at the last position and the first
`length - 1` positions are a heap again; the caller is what shortens the sequence, or leaves the element there.
Fewer than two elements do nothing.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing.

items.name: SortHeap
items.signature: pub func SortHeap<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Turns the heap `items` into a sorted sequence, smallest first.
doc.markdown:
Turns the heap `items` into a sorted sequence, smallest first.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; it must already be a heap, which `MakeHeap` is what makes it. Repeated
popping, which is exactly heapsort.
A sequence that is not a heap does not fail; it comes out rearranged and not sorted.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Makes O(n log n) comparisons and allocates nothing. Equal elements may be reordered.

items.name: IsHeap
items.signature: pub func IsHeap<T>(items: T[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `items` is arranged as a max-heap.
doc.markdown:
Whether `items` is arranged as a max-heap.
`items` is borrowed and read. An empty sequence and a single element are heaps, there being no pair to violate
the property.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether the sequence satisfies the heap property throughout

items.name: IsHeapUntil
items.signature: pub func IsHeapUntil<T>(items: T[..]) -> uint

doc.summary: How much of `items` from the front is arranged as a max-heap.
doc.markdown:
How much of `items` from the front is arranged as a max-heap.
`items` is borrowed and read. Returns the length when the whole sequence is a heap, and otherwise the index of
the first element larger than its parent.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the answer and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: how many leading elements satisfy the heap property

items.name: MakeHeapBy
items.signature: pub func MakeHeapBy<T>(items: var T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering)

doc.summary: Rearranges `items` into a max-heap under `compare`.
doc.markdown:
Rearranges `items` into a max-heap under `compare`.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `compare` must be a strict weak ordering. Fewer than two elements are
already a heap.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `compare` does.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

items.name: PushHeapBy
items.signature: pub func PushHeapBy<T>(items: var T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering)

doc.summary: Restores the heap property under `compare` after an element has been appended to `items`.
doc.markdown:
Restores the heap property under `compare` after an element has been appended to `items`.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; everything before its last element must already be a heap.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever
`compare` does.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

items.signature: pub func PopHeapBy<T>(items: var T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering)

doc.summary: Moves the largest element of `items` under `compare` to its end and restores the heap over the rest.
doc.markdown:
Moves the largest element of `items` under `compare` to its end and restores the heap over the rest.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. The caller is what shortens the sequence afterwards.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

items.name: SortHeapBy
items.signature: pub func SortHeapBy<T>(items: var T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering)

doc.summary: Turns the heap `items` into a sequence sorted by `compare`, smallest first.
doc.markdown:
Turns the heap `items` into a sequence sorted by `compare`, smallest first.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten and must already be a heap under the same comparison.
Cannot fail. Makes O(n log n) comparisons and allocates nothing beyond whatever `compare` does. Equivalent
elements may be reordered.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

items.name: IsHeapBy
items.signature: pub func IsHeapBy<T>(items: T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `items` is arranged as a max-heap under `compare`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `items` is arranged as a max-heap under `compare`.
`items` is borrowed and read. An empty sequence and a single element are heaps.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `compare` does.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

doc.returns: whether the sequence satisfies the heap property throughout under `compare`

items.signature: pub func IsHeapUntilBy<T>(items: T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> uint

doc.summary: How much of `items` from the front is arranged as a max-heap under `compare`.
doc.markdown:

`items` is borrowed and read. Returns the length when the whole sequence is a heap, and otherwise the index of

doc.summary: The indices of the smallest and largest elements of `items`, in one pass.
doc.markdown:

`items` is borrowed and read; `smallest` and `largest` are written only when this reports true. Reports false for
an empty slice and writes neither. Ties go to the earliest index on both ends, exactly as the single-ended

items.name: Reverse
items.signature: pub func Reverse<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Reverses the order of `items` in place.
doc.markdown:
Reverses the order of `items` in place.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. An empty slice and a single element are already reversed, so neither
is a special case.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, making half as many exchanges, and allocates nothing.

items.name: Rotate
items.signature: pub func Rotate<T>(items: var T[..], middle: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Rotates `items` left so that the element at `middle` becomes the first.
doc.markdown:
Rotates `items` left so that the element at `middle` becomes the first.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. A `middle` of zero or of the whole length leaves the order alone;
anything past the length is refused, since there is no such element to bring to the front.
Done as three reversals — the front, the back, then the whole — which needs no scratch storage and touches
every element at most twice.
Reports false only for a `middle` past the length.
Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.

params.name: middle
params.markdown: the index that becomes the new first element

doc.returns: whether `middle` was a usable index

items.name: Fill
items.signature: pub func Fill<T>(items: var T[..], value: T)

doc.summary: Writes `value` into every position of `items`.
doc.markdown:
Writes `value` into every position of `items`.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `value` is read by value and copied into each position. An empty slice
writes nothing.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.

params.name: value
params.markdown: the value to write to every element

items.name: CopyTo
items.signature: pub func CopyTo<T>(destination: var T[..], source: T[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Copies `source` into `destination`, front to back.
doc.markdown:
Copies `source` into `destination`, front to back.
`destination` is borrowed mutably and written; `source` is borrowed and read. Reports false when the two lengths
differ, having written nothing: a partial copy is worse than a refused one, since the caller cannot tell how far
it got.
The two must not overlap, unless `destination` begins at or before `source`. Use `MoveTo` where they might.
Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
Overlapping the wrong way silently copies elements that were already overwritten.
doc.returns: whether `destination` was long enough

items.name: MoveTo
items.signature: pub func MoveTo<T>(destination: var T[..], source: T[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Copies `source` into `destination`, correctly however the two overlap.
doc.markdown:
Copies `source` into `destination`, correctly however the two overlap.
`destination` is borrowed mutably and written; `source` is borrowed and read. Reports false when the two lengths
differ, having written nothing.
Copies back to front when `destination` starts after `source`, and front to back otherwise, which is what makes
shifting a run of elements along its own storage safe in either direction.
Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether `destination` was long enough

items.name: Unique
items.signature: pub func Unique<T>(items: var T[..]) -> uint

doc.summary: Collapses each run of adjacent equal elements in `items` to one, and reports how many are left.
doc.markdown:
Collapses each run of adjacent equal elements in `items` to one, and reports how many are left.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. Only *adjacent* duplicates go: on a sorted slice that removes every
duplicate, and on an unsorted one it removes only the runs, which is the useful behaviour rather than a
compromise — it makes this the second half of sort-then-unique without paying for a second sort.
Relative order among the survivors is preserved, nothing is resized, and what lies past the reported length is
unspecified.
Requires `==` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: how many elements are left after collapsing each run of equal neighbours to one

items.name: RemoveValue
items.signature: pub func RemoveValue<T>(items: var T[..], value: T) -> uint

doc.summary: Removes every element of `items` equal to `value`, and reports how many are left.
doc.markdown:
Removes every element of `items` equal to `value`, and reports how many are left.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `value` is read by value. Survivors are compacted toward the front in
their original order, nothing is resized, and what lies past the reported length is unspecified.
Requires `==` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing.

params.name: value
params.markdown: the value to remove every occurrence of

doc.returns: how many elements are left

items.name: RemoveWhere
items.signature: pub func RemoveWhere<T>(items: var T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> uint

doc.summary: Removes every element of `items` that `predicate` accepts, and reports how many are left.
doc.markdown:
Removes every element of `items` that `predicate` accepts, and reports how many are left.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `predicate` is called once per element. Survivors are compacted toward
the front in their original order, nothing is resized, and what lies past the reported length is unspecified.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: how many elements are left

items.name: Partition
items.signature: pub func Partition<T>(items: var T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> uint

doc.summary: Moves every element `predicate` accepts to the front of `items`, and reports how many there were.
doc.markdown:
Moves every element `predicate` accepts to the front of `items`, and reports how many there were.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `predicate` is called once per element. Everything before the reported
index satisfies the predicate and everything from it on does not.
Order within each group is *not* preserved: this exchanges elements from both ends inward, which is what keeps it
to one pass and no scratch storage. A caller that needs the original order within each group needs a stable
partition, which needs somewhere to put things.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: the index of the first element that fails `predicate`

items.name: PartitionPoint
items.signature: pub func PartitionPoint<T>(items: T[..], predicate: func(T) -> bool) -> uint

doc.summary: Where the accepted elements of an already-partitioned `items` end.
doc.markdown:
Where the accepted elements of an already-partitioned `items` end.
`items` is borrowed and read; `predicate` is called about as many times as the logarithm of the length. Requires
that every element the predicate accepts comes before every element it rejects — which is what `Partition`
leaves behind, and what a sorted slice is with respect to any threshold predicate.
A slice that is not partitioned this way does not fail; it answers, and the answer is meaningless.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever
`predicate` does.

params.name: predicate
params.markdown: the test each element is put to

doc.returns: the index of the first element that fails `predicate`, assuming the sequence is partitioned

items.name: IsSorted
items.signature: pub func IsSorted<T>(items: T[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `items` is in non-decreasing order.
doc.markdown:
Whether `items` is in non-decreasing order.
`items` is borrowed and read. An empty slice and a single element are sorted, there being no pair to be out of
order. Equal neighbours are in order: this asks for non-decreasing, not strictly increasing.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length, stopping at the first pair out of order, and allocates
nothing.
doc.returns: whether the sequence is in non-descending order

items.name: IsSortedUntil
items.signature: pub func IsSortedUntil<T>(items: T[..]) -> uint

doc.summary: How far `items` is in non-decreasing order.
doc.markdown:
How far `items` is in non-decreasing order.
`items` is borrowed and read. Returns the length of the longest sorted run starting at the front, which is the
whole length when the slice is sorted, and the index of the first element smaller than the one before it
otherwise. An empty slice gives zero and a single element gives one.
Requires `<` on the element type.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the answer and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: how many leading elements are in non-descending order

items.name: LowerBound
items.signature: pub func LowerBound<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint

doc.summary: The first position where `value` could be inserted without breaking the order.
doc.markdown:
The first position where `value` could be inserted without breaking the order.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. This is the index of the first element not less than
`value` — the first equal one when there are equals, and where it would go when there are none. A value larger
than everything gives the length.
Requires `<` on the element type, and requires `items` to be sorted by that order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the first index where `value` could be inserted and keep the order

items.name: UpperBound
items.signature: pub func UpperBound<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint

doc.summary: The last position where `value` could be inserted without breaking the order.
doc.markdown:
The last position where `value` could be inserted without breaking the order.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. This is the index of the first element greater than
`value` — one past the last equal one when there are equals, and the same as `LowerBound` when there are none.
Requires `<` on the element type, and requires `items` to be sorted by that order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the last index where `value` could be inserted and keep the order

items.name: BinarySearch
items.signature: pub func BinarySearch<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of an element of `items` equal to `value`.
doc.markdown:
The index of an element of `items` equal to `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. Reports `none` when no element is equal. When several
are, the one reported is the first of them, which makes the answer depend on the sequence rather than on how the
search happened to divide it.
Requires `<` on the element type, and requires `items` to be sorted by that order. Equality is decided by the
ordering rather than by `==`: two elements neither of which is less than the other are equal here, whatever `==`
would say about them.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the index of a matching element, or `none`; which one is unspecified when several match

items.name: EqualRange
items.signature: pub func EqualRange<T>(items: T[..], value: T) -> uint..uint

doc.summary: The range of positions in `items` holding elements equal to `value`.
doc.markdown:
The range of positions in `items` holding elements equal to `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. The range runs from `LowerBound` to `UpperBound`, so it
is empty when no element is equal — and its `start` is then where the value would be inserted, which is the
answer a caller inserting into a sorted sequence wants.
Requires `<` on the element type, and requires `items` to be sorted by that order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the range of indices holding elements equal to `value`, empty when none does

items.name: IsSortedBy
items.signature: pub func IsSortedBy<T>(items: T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `items` is in non-decreasing order under `compare`.
doc.markdown:
Whether `items` is in non-decreasing order under `compare`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `compare` is called once per neighbouring pair until one is out of order. An empty
slice and a single element are sorted, and equal neighbours are in order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever `compare` does.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

doc.returns: whether the sequence is in non-descending order under `compare`

items.name: IsSortedUntilBy
items.signature: pub func IsSortedUntilBy<T>(items: T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> uint

doc.summary: How far `items` is in non-decreasing order under `compare`.
doc.markdown:
How far `items` is in non-decreasing order under `compare`.
`items` is borrowed and read. Returns the length of the longest sorted run starting at the front, exactly as
`IsSortedUntil` does for the element type's own order.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the answer and allocates nothing beyond whatever `compare` does.

params.name: compare

doc.returns: how many leading elements are in non-descending order under `compare`

doc.markdown:
The first position where `value` could be inserted into `items` under `compare` without breaking the order.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. `compare` must be the order `items` was sorted by.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the logarithm of the length and allocates nothing beyond whatever

The last position where `value` could be inserted into `items` under `compare` without breaking the order.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. `compare` must be the order `items` was sorted by.

doc.returns: the last index where `value` could be inserted and keep the order under `compare`

items.name: BinarySearchBy
items.signature: pub func BinarySearchBy<T>(items: T[..], value: T, compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> uint?

doc.summary: The index of an element of `items` that `compare` calls equal to `value`.
doc.markdown:
The index of an element of `items` that `compare` calls equal to `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. Reports `none` when no element is equal, and the first of
them when several are. `compare` must be the order `items` was sorted by.

items.name: EqualRangeBy
items.signature: pub func EqualRangeBy<T>(items: T[..], value: T, compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> uint..uint

doc.summary: The range of positions in `items` holding elements `compare` calls equal to `value`.
doc.markdown:
The range of positions in `items` holding elements `compare` calls equal to `value`.
`items` is borrowed and read; `value` is read by value. Empty when no element is equal, with its `start` at the
position the value would be inserted. `compare` must be the order `items` was sorted by.

items.name: Sort
items.signature: pub func Sort<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Puts `items` into non-decreasing order.
doc.markdown:
Puts `items` into non-decreasing order.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. Fewer than two elements are already sorted, so the data pointer is
never read in that case and an empty view is not a special case.
Requires `<` on the element type, as a strict weak ordering. Equal elements may be reordered: this is not stable.
Cannot fail. Makes O(n log n) comparisons for every input, uses O(1) storage beyond the sequence, and recurses
O(log n) deep.

items.name: SortDescending
items.signature: pub func SortDescending<T>(items: var T[..])

doc.summary: Puts `items` into non-increasing order.
doc.markdown:
Puts `items` into non-increasing order.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten. An ascending sort followed by a reversal, rather than a mirrored copy
of every helper below: threading a direction flag through the partition and both fallbacks would cost a branch in
the innermost comparison, and duplicating the helpers would double the amount of subtle index arithmetic to
maintain, all for one extra linear pass. Sorting is unstable in either direction, so reversing costs nothing in
ordering either.
Requires `<` on the element type. Equal elements may be reordered.
Cannot fail. Makes O(n log n) comparisons and uses O(1) storage beyond the sequence.

items.name: NthElement
items.signature: pub func NthElement<T>(items: var T[..], n: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Puts the element that belongs at `n` in a fully sorted `items` at `n`, and partitions around it.
doc.markdown:
Puts the element that belongs at `n` in a fully sorted `items` at `n`, and partitions around it.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `n` is read by value. Afterwards everything before `n` is at most the
element at `n` and everything after is at least it. Neither side is ordered any further, which is the whole
point: this is what to reach for when only one order statistic is wanted — a median, a percentile — because it
is linear on average where a full sort is not.
Reports false, changing nothing, when `n` is not an index into `items`. That is the only way this fails.
Quickselect over the same partition `Sort` uses, but iterative: only one side of a partition can contain `n`, so
there is nothing to recurse into and the stack stays flat. The same depth budget bounds the worst case at
O(n log n), against O(n) on average.
Requires `<` on the element type. Equal elements may be reordered.

params.name: n
params.markdown: the index whose element should end up in its sorted place

doc.returns: whether `n` was a usable index

items.name: PartialSort
items.signature: pub func PartialSort<T>(items: var T[..], count: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Puts the `count` smallest elements of `items` in order at its front.
doc.markdown:
Puts the `count` smallest elements of `items` in order at its front.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `count` is read by value. The first `count` positions hold the
smallest elements in non-decreasing order, and the rest hold everything else in no particular order.
Reports false, changing nothing, when `count` is larger than the length. A `count` of zero succeeds and does
nothing.
A max-heap over the first `count` elements, which each later element is compared against and displaces only if it
is smaller: O(n log count) comparisons, against the O(n log n) a full sort would cost. That is worth having when
`count` is much smaller than the length and not otherwise.
Requires `<` on the element type. Equal elements may be reordered.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many of the smallest elements to place

doc.returns: whether `count` was a usable length

items.name: SortBy
items.signature: pub func SortBy<T>(items: var T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering)

doc.summary: Puts `items` into the order `compare` describes, smallest first.
doc.markdown:
Puts `items` into the order `compare` describes, smallest first.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `compare` is called O(n log n) times and must be a strict weak
ordering, exactly as `<` must be. Equivalence is derived from it alone, so the element type need not define any
operator at all.
Cannot fail. Makes O(n log n) comparisons for every input, uses O(1) storage beyond the sequence, and recurses
O(log n) deep. Equal elements may be reordered: this is not stable.

items.signature: pub func SortDescendingBy<T>(items: var T[..], compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering)

doc.summary: Puts `items` into the reverse of the order `compare` describes.
doc.markdown:
Puts `items` into the reverse of the order `compare` describes.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `compare` is called O(n log n) times. An ascending sort followed by a
reversal, for the same reason `SortDescending` is.
Cannot fail. Makes O(n log n) comparisons and uses O(1) storage beyond the sequence. Equal elements may be
reordered.

params.name: compare
params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

items.name: NthElementBy
items.signature: pub func NthElementBy<T>(items: var T[..], n: uint, compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> bool

doc.summary: Puts the element that belongs at `n` under `compare` at `n`, and partitions around it.
doc.markdown:
Puts the element that belongs at `n` under `compare` at `n`, and partitions around it.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `n` is read by value; `compare` must be a strict weak ordering.
Exactly `NthElement`, with the order supplied rather than taken from the element type.
Reports false, changing nothing, when `n` is not an index into `items`.
O(n) comparisons on average and O(n log n) at worst. Equivalent elements may be reordered.

params.name: n
params.markdown: the index whose element should end up in its sorted place

params.markdown: how two elements order against each other

doc.returns: whether `n` was a usable index

items.signature: pub func PartialSortBy<T>(items: var T[..], count: uint, compare: func(T, T) -> Ordering) -> bool

doc.summary: Puts the `count` smallest elements of `items` under `compare` in order at its front.
doc.markdown:
Puts the `count` smallest elements of `items` under `compare` in order at its front.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `count` is read by value; `compare` must be a strict weak ordering.
Exactly `PartialSort`, with the order supplied rather than taken from the element type.
Reports false, changing nothing, when `count` is larger than the length.
O(n log count) comparisons. Equivalent elements may be reordered.

items.name: RequiredScratch
items.signature: pub func RequiredScratch(length: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: How much scratch storage a stable sort of `length` elements needs.
doc.markdown:
How much scratch storage a stable sort of `length` elements needs.
`length` is read by value. The answer is `length` itself: a merge writes its output somewhere other than either
of the two runs it reads, and the last merge reads the whole sequence.
Written as a function rather than left to the reader so that a caller sizing a buffer does not have to know that,
and so that it stays right if it ever stops being the whole length.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many elements are to be sorted

doc.returns: how many elements of working storage a stable sort of that length needs

items.name: StableSort
items.signature: pub func StableSort<T>(items: var T[..], scratch: var T[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Puts `items` into non-decreasing order, leaving equal elements in the order they were in.
doc.markdown:
Puts `items` into non-decreasing order, leaving equal elements in the order they were in.
`items` is borrowed mutably and rewritten; `scratch` is borrowed mutably and used as working storage, and what it
holds afterwards is unspecified. Fewer than two elements are already sorted and need no scratch at all.
Reports false, changing nothing, when `scratch` is shorter than `RequiredScratch(items.length)`. That is the only
way this fails.
Requires `<` on the element type, as a strict weak ordering.
Makes O(n log n) comparisons and moves for every input — there is no bad case — and allocates nothing.

params.name: scratch
params.markdown: working storage of at least `RequiredScratch(items.length)` elements

doc.returns: whether `scratch` was large enough; the sequence is untouched when it was not
